To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in a model with no commitment, a power-sharing agreement can be established among power systems with low to moderate risk of participants leaving the pool, 2) in a model where a market operator can observe production fluctuations, the risk of participants leaving can be reduced to zero, and 3) in a model without an impartial market operator, establishing quasi-marketing for excess electricity trading among power systems helps to establish a power-sharing agreement.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the second-best coordination of power systems that are connected through bilateral electricity sharing agreements.
the second best coordination in electricity-sharing agreements among connected power systems in developing countries, where there are no institutional arrangements to coordinate power systems.
the second-best coordination improvements that can be achieved in the short run with voluntary electricity-sharing agreements in developing countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no single solution to the problem of coordination among electricity systems. Rather there is a range of solutions that are more or less efficient, depending on the circumstances of the particular case.

there is a lot to be done in terms of electricity market reforms and the establishment of efficient and transparent electricity markets, but in the absence of this there is still scope for improving electricity sharing in developing countries.
there are no easy solutions, but that some progress can be made.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the coordination among power systems can be improved through the use of quasi-markets for electricity trading.
, in the absence of an efficient institutional framework for electricity markets, there is a scope for second best coordination improvements through bilateral agreements among power systems.
, in the absence of an effective institutional arrangement for coordination among power systems, a voluntary electricity-sharing agreement can be established to achieve a second-best outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of participants leaving an agreement is a crucial determinant of the extent to which electricity sharing can improve efficiency in the presence of market power.

the second-best coordination improvements are achievable even in the presence of a high level of uncertainty in electricity production, provided that the participants have a high level of confidence in each other’s ability and willingness to honor their commitments.
, even in the absence of institutional coordination, there is a role for market-based arrangements in electricity sharing.
